text.p: U.S. trade expert Fred Bergsten on Tuesday sharply criticised U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin for inconsistent trade and exchange rate policies towards Japan and called for action to stem the dollar rise.

"The Treasury has been particularly vocal about avoiding any new Japanese surplus rise. The only way to do that is to avoid the yen getting any weaker," Bergsten, who is director of the Institute for International Economics, told Reuters Financial Television.
In Tokyo last week, Rubin urged Japan to guard against resurgence of its trade surplus, but said a stronger Japanese currency was not the best way to do so.
"I'm afraid Secretary Rubin has said some things that sound very inconsistent," Bergsten said.
U.S. authorities were correct in calling for a curb on the Japanese trade surplus, but a stronger yen was necessary to achieve it, he added.
"If the yen continues to weaken ... particularly at levels like we have now, the Japanese trade surplus will definitely rise to a new record level over the next year or two," he said.

Bergsten said Rubin's calls for a lower Japanese trade surplus were implicitly calling for a stronger yen. The fact that he was unwilling to say so explicitly was confusing the market and was contributing to yen weakness, he added.

He said that short-term fundamentals favored the dollar, so there was no fear that the dollar would fall sharply, even if, for example, there was intervention by members of the Group of Seven industrialized nations.
"This is an ideal situation for the G7 ... or the U.S. authorities or both to try to at least moderate the rise of the dollar and hopefully start a correction in the other direction," he said.
He called on the G7 to follow up on its Berlin statement calling for a cap on the dollar rise.
"The credibility of the G7 is definitely at stake. The G7 said they wanted to cap the dollar, particularly against the yen. They have not done anything to implement their statement," he said.
